title: Ferguson traces why Asia’s financial shock cut output more sharply than Latin America’s
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Vice Chairman Roger Ferguson used the 1997–99 crises to ask why a region with high savings, low inflation and a record of rapid growth suffered the larger downturn. Speaking in Boston on 7 January 2000, he compared five emerging Asian economies with Brazil, Argentina and Mexico. He placed particular weight on a sudden reassessment of Asian financial institutions. Once the size and quality of the credit they had extended came into doubt, overseas investors withdrew and domestic firms lost access to finance just as demand was collapsing. The speech offers competing explanations and comparative evidence. Its policy implications concern banking supervision, currency regimes and crisis management. It gives no view on the next US policy-rate decision.

The first exhibit sets domestic output against crisis timing. Thai GDP fell more than 10% from its local 1997 peak, Malaysian GDP about 10%, Indonesian GDP more than 15% and Korean GDP around 8%. The Philippines lost roughly 3%. For Thailand, the comparison uses the rebound in the second quarter of 1997 even though output had been higher in 1996. The Latin American panel uses a common base in the second quarter of 1998. Brazilian GDP declined about 3% into the end of 1998, then recovered in the first half of 1999. The real had floated in January and lost roughly a third of its value over six months. Argentina, which maintained its peg, lost around 5% of output from mid-1998 to mid-1999. The country with the larger currency decline did not experience the larger output loss. The comparison also captures differences in trading partners and how policy responded before the float.

The external accounts show why the Asian adjustment was so contractionary. Thailand moved from a current-account deficit near 8% of GDP in 1996 to a surplus around 12% in 1998. Dollar export receipts changed little, while the import bill fell about 40%. Across the five Asian economies, Exhibit 2A puts the improvement in the current account at $123.2 billion and the decline in merchandise imports at $116.6 billion. For the three Latin American economies, the estimated current-account improvement from 1998 to 1999 was $13.3 billion, with aggregate imports barely changed. The Latin American figures include contemporary forecasts for 1999. The comparison therefore uses different lengths of time and, for one region, estimates still subject to revision.

The retreat of credit was visible in new transactions. Gross private flows to four Asian economies fell from about $28 billion in the second half of 1996 to $4 billion in the second half of 1998. New bank loans fell almost two-thirds and bond issuance more than 90%. This measure counts loans received and new debt and equity issuance, excluding interbank flows. It captures drying-up access to new funding, while leaving repayments, banks' interbank exposures and net capital flight outside the measure. New financing recovered in both regions in the first half of 1999. Those definitions matter when relating a funding shock to subsequent exchange rates or GDP.

Ferguson tested whether familiar macro indicators could rank the countries' vulnerabilities in advance. Asian budget balances and growth generally looked healthy, while Brazil had carried a fiscal deficit above 5% of GDP. The Philippines had one of the clearest signs of currency appreciation relative to its own history but experienced one of the milder Asian contractions. The banking comparison gave a different ordering. Thai domestic savings near 35% of GDP, plus foreign savings reflected in a current-account deficit around 8%, meant an unusually large flow of resources required allocation. Separately, the stock of bank claims on the private sector was around 100% of Thai GDP and 60% in Korea, compared with roughly 20% in the three Latin American economies. Even equally competent banks would expose more output to errors in credit assessment when their balance sheets were that large.

Sovereign ratings reflected how far investors' assessment changed. Standard & Poor's cut Thailand four notches, Indonesia six and Korea ten. Argentina and Mexico retained their BB ratings, while Brazil fell one notch. This is evidence about changes in perceived creditworthiness, with no direct estimate of the price of sovereign risk or which announcement triggered the repricing. The Latin American countries had already experienced the 1994–95 peso crisis. Changes to supervision and banking practices, and investors' prior awareness of vulnerabilities, could each have reduced the size of the surprise.

The timing of policy and the location of foreign demand offer two further explanations. Latin American authorities generally raised rates earlier. Thailand intervened to defend its currency and delayed more aggressive tightening, running down reserves before relief came through the exchange rate. Ferguson favoured acting promptly when defending a peg or allowing adjustment through depreciation. Mexico could let the peso weaken and sold about three-quarters of its exports to a booming US economy, sales worth roughly a fifth of Mexican output. Several Asian economies faced weaker Japanese import demand and lending from Japanese banks. The distinction matters for historical research. A smaller recession after an early rate increase could reflect the availability of a strong export market, a healthier banking system or the fact that the country came under pressure later. Ferguson argues for greater disclosure and stronger credit assessment without claiming these comparisons identify a single cause of the regional gap.

questions.question: Did a surprise about domestic banks lead the fall in external finance, or did banks deteriorate after international lenders pulled back?
questions.detail: Date bank-loss disclosures, ratings actions, changes in sovereign spreads, international issuance and cross-border loan renewals. Separate gross new lending from maturing debt and interbank exposures absent from Exhibit 3. If repricing came before new information about local credit losses and affected the same foreign lenders' borrowers elsewhere, a common funding shock would deserve more weight than a purely domestic reassessment.

questions.question: How much of Latin America's smaller contraction can be attributed to exchange-rate flexibility and the speed of intervention?
questions.detail: Reconstruct reserve losses, short rates, exchange-rate moves and domestic credit using comparable windows around each country's initial pressure. Condition on pre-existing foreign-currency debt, banking health and trading-partner growth. Compare countries with similar exposures. A bank or borrower with unhedged dollar debts could experience a much larger contraction after the same depreciation, making the currency regime alone an unreliable guide to outcomes.

questions.question: Was the current-account improvement a consequence of scarce finance, collapsing domestic spending or external demand?
questions.detail: Decompose imports and exports into prices and volumes and separate inputs for exporters from goods destined for local buyers. Check whether bank-dependent sectors lost imports and output first, and whether exporters selling to the United States fared better than similar exporters selling to Japan. Use realised Latin American data alongside the 1999 forecasts available to Ferguson to isolate revisions from differences in economic mechanisms.
